events.excerpt: Russia's central bank is rapidly widening the list of firms allowed to trade crypto, as the country's two biggest lenders prepare to sell Bitcoin and other coins to ordinary customers before the end of the year. The Bank of Russia added a 17th company, Prosto LLC, to its register of crypto exchange providers on Thursday, according to a notice on the regulator's website . The register had four members when it opened on 6 October. The separate register of digital depositories, which record who owns which coins, now has eight. The registrations put into practice a law "On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights", which took effect on 1 September and brings crypto trading inside Russia's regulated financial system for the first time. Sberbank and VTB hold both licences Sberbank and VTB, Russia's largest state-controlled banks, were among the first five digital depositories approved on 6 October, the central bank said . VTB was also listed as a crypto exchange provider that day. Sberbank joined the exchange register on 12 October, Interfax reported . Holding both statuses lets a bank buy and sell crypto in its own name and keep the record of clients' holdings. events.excerpt: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight relate

events.excerpt: For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework . For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators. What a Korean user sees when they sign up The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: " By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy. " A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. events.excerpt: EIP-8288 proposes recursive aggregation under a fixed protocol-level verification key. One backend choice worth exploring is whether recursive steps should support several approved proof sizes, so that small aggregates can use a smaller proving relation. I implemented this kind of heterogeneous recursion in Parano1d, where small and large recursive state-transition proofs already run on a public mainnet. The construction uses a finite authenticated bank of verifier classes. I recently published the paper , and I think the mechanism is relevant to the aggregation backend being discussed here. Carrying deferred checks across classes A verifier class fixes a relation, its constraint matrix, polynomial commitment parameters and transcript layout. Classes share a public accumulator layout, while their witness dimensions, matrices and commitment geometries can differ. The permitted classes and their ordered bank digest are authenticated public parameters. The part that needs care is deferred verification. Replaying a parent proof leaves a matrix-evaluation claim that must remain accounted for through subsequent recursive steps, including steps using another class. The bank has one accumulator lane per class. At step k , let i_k be the current proof’s class and i_{k-1} its parent’s clas
events.headline: Paranoid EIP-8288: heterogeneous recursion with an authenticated class bank

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, We just opened the public testnet of Luggom, a Cosmos SDK app-chain with one job: turn a real tax payment into money you own, proven end to end with TLSNotary. No KYC. No third parties. The bank session never leaves the user's device. ## Why another chain? Because Cosmos is at its best when an app-chain brings a new kind of user. Luggom brings the taxpayer. There is no subsidy and no token sale. The inflow is a real payment that already leaves people's accounts every year. The chain's job is to prove it happened and mint against it. ## How it works 1. The user pays a real tax at their bank, as always. 2. TLSNotary proves the paid receipt without exposing the session. 3. The notary signs the attestation; the chain verifies it and mints. 4. Each receipt mines exactly once (payment_id + proof_commitment anti-replay). The desktop app (Tauri/Rust) builds the proof request and signs locally. The seed never leaves the device. What is live - chain-id: `luggom-test` - RPC: `https://rpc.luggom.com` - LCD: `https://lcd.luggom.com` - API: `https://api.luggom.com` - Notary: `wss://notary.luggom.com/session` - Full nodes: open (p2p 26656) — seed `1530baa7b3a07e0cab8dc81c9c08fccc51a47471@62.146.183.122:26656` - Validators: by invitation (the operator funds 200 testnet LUG) - App +
events.headline: Luggom — a Cosmos SDK app-chain where you mine LUG by paying real taxes (public testnet)

events.excerpt: Hi all, Thanks to @aelowsson @julian @b-wagn @GottfriedHerold , since this builds directly on LUCID, the criticism thread and the ticket-first threshold IBE design. Also a kind request for review on this work. I’ve been wondering how much the “free option” in encrypted mempools is actually worth, and what happens if you try to take it away. The short version is in the TL;DR. The full treatment, with proofs, is in the paper, and the Lean 4 formalization is linked below. Edit (Oct 28): BSR is now instantiated on Gottfried’s ticket-first threshold IBE design, and the timing numbers are corrected for the ePBS bid commitment. Details in the reply below. TL;DR If a sender can decide whether to reveal after seeing new information, they hold a free option. I bound its value and show what happens when you try to remove it. Fees alone don’t price it well, because senders can use many conditional commitments. Taking the option from senders just moves it to committee members. I propose Blind Simultaneous Release (BSR), which fixes the executed set before anyone can condition on new information. It uses only hashes, so it is post-quantum. It plugs into the ticket-first threshold IBE design as a release layer for the committee’s key shares. Paper: Reveal-Optionality-BSR.pdf (395.8 KB), or you
events.headline: Reveal optionality in encrypted mempools: how big is the sender’s free option, and a post-quantum way to remove it

events.excerpt: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoret

events.excerpt: This post follows Informed Diffusion: making home builders publish fast (2026). Author: @cskiraly Update, 29 October 2026: this post stays as published. Its text is kept current, with the latest results, on notes.ethereum.org , and each version, with its data and scripts, at eth-networking-studies . SEACAST’s specification and its releases are at informed-diffusion-spec ; news is posted as replies to this topic. TL;DR Ethereum has more and more large objects to broadcast, and little time for each. Today’s payloads are small and datacenters carry them, which is much of why mainnet is in time, but payloads grow (with gas increase and block-level access lists, BALs) and timelines shrink (with quick slots). Execution proofs and consensus blocks with post-quantum signatures may soon join the large-message club too. Today’s delivery method (gossipsub) sits far from being optimal : every node waits for the whole object before passing it on, and receives several copies of it. From a builder at home, the last nodes receive a 1 MiB payload seconds late. Not every node needs every byte. With data-availability sampling, a node is to receive its samples of an object, not the object. PeerDAS’s 128 column topics are only one way of doing sampled diffusion; RowDAS and FullDAS are other examples.
events.headline: SEACAST: fast, lean, sampled broadcast for Ethereum, with an executable spec and a formal model

events.excerpt: Today, we are expanding our web application firewall (WAF) by adding two new capabilities: full transaction detections and response rules. Full transaction detections evaluate each HTTP request alongside its response to identify evidence of exploitation. It helps answer both "Does this request look malicious?" and "What happened when the application handled it?" Response rules can then block the origin’s response before it reaches the requester. These are valuable protections because the latest frontier models are uncovering vulnerabilities buried deep in widely used software, giving defenders clarity on what to fix — and attackers new paths to exploit. The recent php2shell vulnerability shows the stakes: a flaw in a common software component can put applications across the Internet at risk. AI agents scanning for vulnerabilities can be extremely persistent, adapting payloads using feedback, and chaining vulnerabilities, credentials, and permissions. An application's response can reveal whether an attempt worked and give an attacker information that helps them go deeper. Inspecting incoming requests remains essential for stopping recognizable attacks before they reach an application. But some threats become clear only when the request is considered alongside what the origin retur
events.headline: Introducing full transaction detection for Cloudflare WAF

events.excerpt: Opening community discussion on URC-5: Token Venue Policy . Some tokens recommend particular liquidity pools or restrict trading to supported venues, often because their mechanics depend on a Uniswap v4 hook (INDEX, STANDARD, FWA, etc). Without a shared way to discover those policies, routers and frontends need token-specific integrations and may otherwise offer unsupported routes. Anecdotally, STANDARD and FWA prevented a lot of trading volume due to routers routing to restricted pools and required bespoke integrations for both. URC-5 defines IVenuePolicy , a token-level interface for declaring canonical v4 pools, distinguishing Preferred and Enforced policies, and exposing directional permissions for other liquidity venues. It also specifies how routers, aggregators, and frontends should interpret those declarations. Transfer-time enforcement remains token-specific. We’d appreciate input from hook developers, token teams, routers, aggregators, and frontend implementers. 6 posts - 4 participants Read full topic
events.headline: URC-5: Token Venue Policy

events.excerpt: Reth v2.8.0 schedules the Amsterdam hardfork on Hoodi, adds opt-in snap/2 sync and prewarm result reuse, and hardens peer-to-peer networking and RPC. With the opt-in --engine.prewarm-reuse , reth commits prewarmed transaction results instead of re-executing them. This reduced mean latency by 12.35% and raised Mgas/s by 18.58% over 500 replayed blocks ( #27894 ). Per-block proof-worker sizing reduced mean execution time on 300M-gas BAL blocks by 8.41% ( #27196 ). RPC response compression no longer cuts throughput by up to 22x ( #27863 ). Action Required Hoodi operators must upgrade before 26 October 2026 at 17:42:48 UTC. This release schedules Amsterdam on Hoodi at timestamp 1793036568 (epoch 132352) and extends the Hoodi fork IDs through Amsterdam. ( Reth change , Hoodi schedule ) All operators should review the default and behavior changes under Breaking Changes, especially those affecting the gas price oracle, WebSocket origins and the minimum priority fee. Update Priority User Class Priority Payload Builders Medium Non-Payload Builders Medium Breaking Changes Runtime and Configuration Changed the default gas price oracle ignore threshold ( --gpo.ignoreprice ) from 0 to 2 wei to match Geth, so zero-tip transactions no longer pull eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas down to 0. events.excerpt: In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity.
